title: The fake field goal: when the holder and kicker become a backfield (and how Oregon scored before halftime)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files. The backup source (football-film-room, branch "data") couldn't be read: "GitHub access to this repository is not enabled for this session" (HTTP 403). So there's no new miss of yours to fix. It's a new concept tied to Friday's Oregon-Michigan State game. It builds on Lesson 36 (field goals) and Lesson 35 (gadget plays).

The big idea: a field-goal team looks like it will kick. The defense rushes to block it.On a fake, the holder keeps the ball. He runs, throws, or pitches it to the kicker.It works because the defense has sent its players up the middle to block the kick. The outside is nearly empty.

White = offense, moving up toward the end zone. Yellow = defense. The dashed yellow line is the pitch. The solid white line is the kicker's run.

  1. A · The snap. The long snapper (yellow outline) fires the ball 7 yards back. It looks exactly like a real kick.
  2. B · The holder. On a kick he catches the snap and sets the ball down. On a fake he stands up with it.Holders are often backup QBs or punters, so many can throw or pitch.
  3. C · The kicker. He's already moving forward to kick. On this fake he keeps running and takes the pitch.Defenders don't watch the kicker. Nobody is assigned to tackle him.
  4. D · The edge. Outside the wing blocker. The defense packs 9 or more players inside to block the kick, so only 1 or 2 are out here.Get there and it's a footrace.

Friday's real example: just before halftime, Oregon led Michigan State and lined up for a field goal.Holder Bailey Ettridge took the snap and pitched to kicker Gage Hurych. Hurych ran 15 yards for a touchdown.The replay official checked it and upheld the score. Oregon led 17-0 at halftime instead of 13-0.

Why it matters for bets: a fake turns 3 points into 7. That's +4 on the total and +4 on the spread.Friday's 4 extra points before halftime helped push the game to 52, over the board's 45.5 (Market 101, Lesson 58).Fakes are rare, but they come when coaches see a weak spot on film, often right before halftime or on 4th-and-short.

For your Film Room drill: when the field-goal team runs on, your usual call is "kick." Clues for a fake:It's 4th-and-short, so a first down is easy. A wing blocker lines up wider than usual. The holder is a backup QB.The defense has only 10 players on the field, or is rushing everyone inside.If the holder pitches or runs, log it as a run. If he throws, log it as a pass.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 36 showed how a field goal works and why misses swing games. Lesson 35 showed gadget plays that use surprise. A fake field goal is both: the same formation, a different play.

Video: search YouTube for "Oregon fake field goal Gage Hurych Michigan State" and "fake field goal explained."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

quiz.q: On a field-goal try, who usually catches the snap?
quiz.w: The holder catches the snap about 7 yards back and sets it down. On a fake he keeps it.

quiz.q: Why does a fake field goal often get to the edge?
o: The defense packs players inside to block the kick
The ball is snapped to the side
quiz.w: The defense sends 9 or more players up the middle to block the kick. Only 1 or 2 are left outside.

quiz.q: Oregon's fake turned a likely field goal into a TD. How much did that add to the total?
quiz.w: A field goal is 3. A TD plus the extra point is 7. That's 4 more points on the total and the spread.

quiz.q: In your Film Room drill, the holder stands up and pitches to the kicker. What do you log?
quiz.w: A pitch or a run by the holder is a run play. If he throws it, it's a pass.
